problems.location: Concept 1: Evidence-Based Strategies for Retention and Conceptual Integration / block 1
problems.lesson_text: The act of reconstructing a memory trace in response to environmental cues re-consolidates and stabilizes neural representations, insulating them against future interference and decay.
problems.source_text: not in source (the source says only: "Some evidence shows that the act of retrieval itself enhances learning")

problems.location: Concept 4: Workforce Learning Ecologies and Socially Mediated Professional Practice / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Synthesis of learning quadrants (NRC, 2018) and empirical transfer climate factors (Blume et al., 2010; Rouiller & Goldstein, 1993).
problems.source_text: not in source (the source describes learning "that is incidental and informal (i.e., as a side effect of the work), intentional but nonformal (related to work activities), or formal on-the-job and off-the job training and education (Tynjälä, 2008)")
problems.reason: How People Learn II has no 'learning quadrants' framework, and the table's grid and cells such as 'Mandatory job shadowing; HR policy reviews with supervisor' are not in the sources.

problems.location: Concept 1: Evidence-Based Strategies for Retention and Conceptual Integration / block 1
problems.lesson_text: Despite its robust empirical support across ages 4 through adulthood, learners routinely underutilize retrieval.
problems.source_text: Some evidence shows that the act of retrieval itself enhances learning ... However, most of this research has addressed retrieval of relatively simple information (e.g., vocabulary), rather than deep understanding.
problems.reason: The lesson presents retrieval as robustly proven and 'a potent cognitive event', dropping the source's caveat that the evidence mostly covers simple information rather than deep understanding.

problems.location: Concept 1: Evidence-Based Strategies for Retention and Conceptual Integration / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Learners naturally prefer blocked study due to its immediate perceived fluency, but interleaving produces superior long-term inductive classification and mathematical flexibility.
problems.source_text: These results suggest that interleaved study improves learning of highly similar categories (by facilitating between-category comparisons), whereas blocked study improves learning of low-similarity categories (by facilitating within-category comparisons).
problems.reason: The source gives a conditional picture in which blocking helps low-similarity categories, but the lesson says interleaving is simply superior.

problems.location: Concept 1: Evidence-Based Strategies for Retention and Conceptual Integration / block 4
problems.lesson_text: Ionas and colleagues (2012) demonstrated that prior knowledge strictly moderates the efficacy of self-explanation: while learners with established conceptual schemas benefit substantially, novices with inadequate background knowledge experience cognitive overload and performance impairment. For early learners, unassisted discovery and unguided generative tasks fail;
problems.source_text: Moreover, for students who had just a little prior knowledge, using self-explanation seemed to impede rather than support performance.
problems.reason: The source reports one hedged study of college chemistry students, but the lesson turns it into a firm rule ('strictly', 'fail') and stretches it to discovery tasks and early learners.

problems.location: Concept 1: Evidence-Based Strategies for Retention and Conceptual Integration / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Requires formative feedback; ineffective if dropped after a single success
problems.source_text: students who practiced retrieval one time recalled more of the material than students who only read the texts, and the students who repeatedly retrieved the material performed the best.
problems.reason: The source shows that a single retrieval still beats rereading, so calling retrieval ineffective after one success contradicts it.

problems.location: Concept 3: Empirical Affordances and Systems Alignment of Learning Technologies / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Mayer (2016) shows no general transfer to broad cognitive skill tests; benefits are limited to specific academic domain objectives.
problems.source_text: Nevertheless, games may be more effective than alternative approaches for some specific categories of learning outcomes. For example, “shooter” type games have resulted in transferable learning of perceptual attention skills (Mayer, 2016).
problems.reason: The same review reports transferable perceptual attention skills from games, so saying benefits are limited to academic domain objectives contradicts the source.

problems.location: Concept 4: Workforce Learning Ecologies and Socially Mediated Professional Practice / block 3
problems.lesson_text: High transfer persistence; dependent on job autonomy and perceived personal utility.
problems.source_text: Quantifying the benefits of autonomous workplace learning at the organizational level in this way would help to clarify how it works and why it is beneficial; thus far, however, we are not aware of any research on this.
problems.reason: The lesson states high transfer for self-directed learning as an empirical finding, but the source says these benefits have not been studied.

problems.location: Exercise 1.2: Critiquing instructional designs that mistake massed familiarity for durable retrieval practice and elaborative explanation / block 4
problems.lesson_text: Step 3: States that immediate explanation builds conceptual integration regardless of prior knowledge or timing; correct alternative: elaborative explanation is only effective with sufficient prior knowledge and when spaced over time.
problems.source_text: The students who self-explained showed larger gains in comprehension of concepts in the text.
problems.reason: The answer key says explanation works only when spaced over time, but the source reports gains from explaining within a single study session and never ties it to spacing.
